# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Trevor's answer sits a little oddly under "Logs cost little time today": he doesn't say logs cost little, he says today's roughly $600 a month in overtime is the ceiling on what he'd pay, and that point is nearer Omar's "show me the hours" (left on his own) than Faith's "not much time lost"; the per-site group is clean and the names are plain.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and every answer speaks to price or worth.

founder.order_why: Mostly sensible, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I already named my first step, a paid pilot on one site (20-21), so the pilot question belongs right after or inside the commitment step.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and question, which reads as the context being asked twice. Screen 2 (where buyers are) and the context's 'where: US' / US general contractors segment cover the same ground. Screen 22's pilot offer repeats the pilot already given as the commitment in 20-21.
founder.missing: Nothing asked what the price is per: Fresco charges per site per month with unlimited users on the project, and the multi-site and multi-month discounts are what bring it toward $800. Nothing asked whether pushing notes into Procore/ACC is a must-have for the buyer, as opposed to just one more check to clear before buying.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It runs from the time we spend now, to what it's worth, to who signs, to the Procore check, to a pilot, which is how I'd actually work through buying it, though the counter jumps from 2 of 6 to 4 of 6 as if a screen got dropped.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How many active sites we run at once and how many people per site would log in, since that drives the total monthly bill more than the per-site price does; also what we already pay for daily-log tools or add-ons in Procore.

screens.why2: It is a plain question in my own buyer's title, and the hint (two roles at most, a few words each, Nobody counts) is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: Who else at a general contractor has to approve a $1k-a-month-per-site tool is something I have heard in my own sales calls, so I can answer it directly.
screens.why4: There is a free box for roles, Nobody is allowed as an answer and the I'm not sure chip is the right way out for a founder who can't say, so nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: My answer, The CFO; The project executive, fits as typed: two roles under four words each, in my order, with nothing added or reworded.
screens.why7: The box takes at most two roles of at most 4 words each, in my words, beside the named decider, and allows Nobody and the I'm not sure escape, as the card's founder role_list requires.

screens.why1: Right after I named the CFO and the project executive as the people who have to agree, Keel shows the list back so I can confirm it before the stranger's item is built from it.
screens.why2: Superintendent, operations lead, CFO and project executive are the titles I use when I talk to general contractors, and the tags are plain, though the intro repeats the title 'The people involved'.
screens.why3: It asks who at the GC uses it, signs and has to agree, which I know from selling per site to contractors.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and in my words, but the untagged 'Nobody else' sits above two roles tagged 'has to agree', so it reads as a contradiction unless I know it is the fixed first row.
screens.why5: Keel kept my two roles verbatim and in my order, merged the super as the person with the problem, kept the ops lead as the decider, and added no one.
screens.why7: Nobody else is fixed first, the user and the decider are tagged, at most two roles are each tagged 'has to agree' in my words, and the belief can carry both roles joined with 'and'.
screens.instead: Same list, with 'Nobody else' tagged '(only if no one below has to agree)' or greyed out once roles are named: Construction superintendent · has the problem; Contractor operations lead · decides to buy; The CFO · has to agree; The project executive · has to agree.

screens.why1: After naming the operations lead as decider and the CFO and project executive as the ones who must agree, the next step is picking which belief to test, so it is clear why this is asked.
screens.why2: 'Which one do you want to test?' over 'Nobody else' and 'The CFO and the project executive' is plain to me, and the intro says in a line what the stranger will be asked.
screens.why3: I know how a GC buys a per-site tool, so I can tell which belief I hold without guessing.
screens.why4: The two rows are the two real choices, the decider alone or with the two roles I named, they are distinct, and nothing I would pick is missing.
screens.why5: The belief and the bar both carry the CFO and the project executive as I typed them, with the contractor operations lead as the decider, and nothing added or dropped.
screens.why7: Choose offers the decider alone or the decider with every role tagged has to agree, and the belief joins both roles with 'and'; the bar can be supported or refuted on the fixed four, and a stranger's item naming only the CFO is the card's Open point, not a fault.

screens.why1: Right after naming who has to agree, asking what my contractor's side must clear before paying is the obvious next thing to pin down about how Fresco sells.
screens.why2: "What must the buyer's own side clear before they pay" is plain to me, and the hint's example and its "not your own trial or pilot" tell me exactly what kind of step to type.
screens.why3: I know the GC's process from selling to them: someone checks it fits their Procore or ACC setup, and someone looks at where the site videos go before a dollar moves.
screens.why4: The box takes my own steps, and the one chip, I'm not sure, is the honest escape for a founder who doesn't know the buyer's process.
screens.why5: Both of my steps sit there in my own words, in my order, with nothing reworded.
screens.why7: Both steps are brakes on the contractor's side, each a noun phrase under 9 words with its object, neither repeats the other, neither is my own trial or pilot, the biggest comes first, and the time is left for me to type on the next screen.

screens.why1: Right after I named what the buyer's side has to clear, Keel shows me the list back to check before I pick one and give it a time, so it is obvious why it is here.
screens.why2: Both rows are in my own words: a GC checks a tool against Procore, and IT asks for a security review of footage from the site.
screens.why3: I have sat through both of these with every contractor I have pitched, so I can check this list from what I know.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct steps on the contractor's side, nothing silly is on the list, and dropping the trial leaves nothing true missing.
screens.why5: These are the two buyer-side steps I gave, kept in my wording, and the trial I offer was rightly taken off.
screens.why7: Both rows are brakes on the buyer's side that I don't control, each a noun phrase with its object and under 9 words; neither contains the other, none is my offer or the purchase itself, and the integration check comes first as the bigger blocker.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the steps the contractor's side has to clear, it's obvious I now pick one and say how long I think it takes.
screens.why2: A Procore check and a security review of the site videos are exactly how a GC's ops side talks about bringing in a new field tool, and the time box is plain.
screens.why3: I've been through these with the contractors I sell to, so I can pick the step and put a number on it from my own deals.
screens.why4: The two steps are distinct and in my words, and 'I'm not sure' is the right escape for a founder who can't put a time on it.
screens.why5: Both rows are the ones I kept after the trial row was dropped, and the belief carries my own 2 weeks, nothing Keel invented.
screens.why7: Both rows are brakes on the buyer's side, not my offer, and my typed 2 weeks becomes the band edge; the bar counts under 2 weeks or not needed as for and the longer bands as against, so the belief can hold or fail, and 'I'm not sure' is the founder's escape.

screens.why1: After who decides, the price and what the buyer's side must clear, asking for the first step I want the contractor to take is the obvious last commercial question before strangers see it.
screens.why2: Plain to me: the question asks two things, the step and its cost, but the hint folds them into one short step with where the money goes, and 'pay for a pilot' is exactly how I talk about selling to a GC.
screens.why3: It asks about my own sales motion, a paid pilot on one site, which I know cold.
screens.why4: A box to type in with the single 'I'm not sure' chip, which is the founder-side escape the card allows and which would leave the dimension out.
screens.why5: My words 'start a paid pilot on one site' go in as typed, and the hint names my decider, the contractor operations lead, without changing what I sell.
screens.why7: The box asks for one first step of at most 9 words that says where the money goes, and it promises a free smaller step on the next screen because my step costs money, exactly as the card's founder step says, with 'I'm not sure' allowed.

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step, Keel shows how strangers will hear it and drafts the free smaller step a paid pilot calls for; that is the right place for it.
screens.why2: My step reads plainly, but the smaller-step field shows a whole answer, "Yes, after a free look at it on sample data first", instead of a short phrase. "Sample data" is software talk; to a GC ops lead "a sample job" would be plainer.
screens.why3: Whether an ops lead would run a paid pilot on one site, or want a look first, is exactly what I know from selling to general contractors.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and complete: a firm yes to my step, a soft yes after a free look, probably not, and no, with no escape, as there should be.
screens.why5: "Start a paid pilot on one site" is mine word for word, but "a free look at it on sample data" is Keel's drafting: "sample data" is a detail I never wrote, and "it" never says it is Fresco.
screens.why7: The served list fits the card: my step whole, then "Probably, after {smaller step} first", then probably not, then no; the belief can hold or fail. But the smaller_step field holds an answer frame ("Yes, after ... first") instead of a noun phrase of at most 9 words, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Your step: start a paid pilot on one site · Or a smaller step first: a free walkthrough on a sample job — Yes, I'd start a paid pilot on one site · Probably, after a free walkthrough on a sample job first · Probably not · No

screens.why1: Right after I named my first real step (a paid pilot on one site), and before the study goes out, it makes sense to ask whether strangers should be offered that pilot.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with Yes or No is plain to me as a founder, and the hint says exactly what the respondent sees and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is entirely my own call, and I know the answer: I want contractors on a paid site pilot.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, the two don't overlap, and no escape is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: I typed 'start a paid pilot on one site', but the line strangers get, 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.', drops both 'paid' and 'one site', so a superintendent may say yes to a free try rather than to my paid one-site pilot.
screens.instead: Offer your pilot at the end: "Would you start a paid pilot of this on one of your sites? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my supers the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer and before launch.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, voice, typing, credits and text-message delivery into one block, and my recorded pick talks about a 'face' while the screen only offers voices, so I had to read it twice to see what I was choosing.
screens.why3: As the founder I can decide which voice my superintendents hear by listening to the two 5-second samples.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a sample and one preselected, cover the choice, and the hint says the text-and-tap route is there either way.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed about Fresco, superintendents or the contractor, and no product detail leaks.
screens.instead: Who should read your questions aloud to construction superintendents? (They can also read and tap.) Options: Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s, with one line below: 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Choosing how the operations leads at the general contractors will answer is the natural last setup step, right after choosing who asks the superintendents.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose are plain to me, and each option says in one line what the person on the other end does.
screens.why3: I know my buyers are busy operations leads at GCs who would rather tap through a link than sit on a video call, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choices, and my pick of Read and tap is there as written.
screens.why5: The question says contractors while the earlier screens called this group the contractor operations lead, so the wording drifted a little from the role I set.
screens.instead: How should the contractor operations leads answer? (AI interviewer Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: This is the last step of sending interviews, so asking who gets a link is the obvious thing to settle here, right after how contractors should answer.
screens.why2: It's clear enough, but 'Who gets a link?' doesn't say whether it means the contractor ops leads from the previous screen or my superintendents, and 'the Contacts page' assumes I know where that is in Keel.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching out to GCs I've met by name, through a list, or by posting in a group, so this is fully mine to answer.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list and one open link in a group are three distinct ways to reach people, each explained in plain words, and my pick of named contacts is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is altered or leaked; it's purely about how I distribute links.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Not holding up, sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it: Price, 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives the count, the n and the bar, but the kicker's 1 TO 8 COUNTED and Existing sacrifice's 5 of 7 when 8 answered need a second look to see who was left out and why.
screens.why_b3: The names, the $800 to $1,000 per site a month, the 30 to 60 hours, the Procore check within 2 weeks and the paid pilot on one site are my beliefs in my words.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do: the page never sets the 40-hour median cost against the price buyers would pay, or says whether to cut the price, price per user, or go to a different buyer.
screens.why_b5: No claim reaches past the eight leads, but the low n of 8 is never said, and Not holding up next to Did not hold leaves me guessing whether price could still turn.
screens.instead: Not holding up: your buyers say supers already spend about 40 hours a site a month on the log, yet only 1 of 8 leads would pay $800, so test a lower price or show them the hours in dollars; that is 8 people, too few to settle it.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 7 spend 30 hours or more per site a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip says what it counts (hours of the daily log per site a month), over how many (one cell per person, 7 counted), and where my bar sits (5 of 7, at least 2 in 3, marker at 5), all at first look.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice and my 30 to 60 hours per site a month on the daily log are mine, but the belief drops 'on commercial jobs' from the superintendents I named, so it is reworded though recognisable.
screens.why_b4: The So line says what this means for me: the cost is real at or above my low, and the open question is willingness to pay, which it sends me to the Price card to answer.
screens.why_b5: The small group is flagged ('a lean, not a call') and Faith's none-as-0 is shown, but Trevor's '10.9 hours' reads as if he said it, when his firm's cost was an amount converted to hours, a precision he never gave.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 contractors spend 30+ hours per site a month (median 40, about $2,200 at $55/hour, more than my $1k price), so the cost is not why Price failed; and show Trevor's answer as the dollar amount he gave, with the conversion to hours stated.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know at once that my price failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each band shows its count marked for or against, my $800 to $1,000 is placed on its band, and the strip shows 1 for, 7 against and the marker at 6 of 8, so I see what is counted, over eight people and where the bar is in one look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Price, and its belief, 'Contractor operations leads would think Fresco worth $800 to $1,000 per site a month', is my range, unit and period exactly as I gave them.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the miss (most chose under $500) and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say what that means for Fresco, for example that the logs cost them more than my price but the buyers don't see it, or that the comments point to a free pilot or per-user pricing.
screens.why_b5: All eight answered and are shown, the count line calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the rule line, chart, strip and each person's mark agree.
screens.instead: Only 1 of 8 buyers would pay $800, yet the last card showed the logs already cost about 40 hours a site a month. The gap is that buyers don't see that cost: show them the hours, and consider a free one-job pilot or pricing per active super, as their comments ask.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', and the So line repeats the same reason, so I know the answer and why at once.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count where Gordon's money would come from, but the strip draws 5 cells (1 against, 4 ghosts) with a bar at '4 of 5' when only 1 person was asked, and the rule line doesn't match the chart's for/against tags, so I have to look twice.
screens.why_b3: It's my buyer (the contractor's operations lead) at my price ($800 to $1,000 per site a month), in my own words, and it doesn't claim I checked a belief I never saw.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' says the call is pending, but it doesn't say this hangs on Price: only 1 of 8 reached my band, so more answers won't reach 5 unless I change the price or find buyers who'd pay it.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said, but 'a lean, not a call' over one person is soft, and the rule line leaves out 'charged to the teams or sites' (for) and grants (against) and counts a 'none' the list doesn't offer.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Gordon reached your $800 and he'd need a new budget line signed off; with 7 of 8 below your price, Ability to pay can't be read until Price moves, so test a lower price or buyers who'd pay $800.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Holding up, sits right beside the number that decides it (6 of 8 as I said or easier, bar 6 of 8, at the bar), so I know it held, though only just.
screens.why_b2: The four answers show their counts and are marked for or against, the 8 answered is plain, and the strip puts the marker on my bar of 6 of 8, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Buyer and payer and keeps my belief whole, with the operations lead deciding and both the CFO and the project executive named; asking only about the CFO is the registry's open choice, not this screen's fault.
screens.why_b4: It says to plan for the CFO in deals and notes that 2 of 8 could sign alone, which tells me to build the CFO into my pilot pitch.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a small group, a lean and not a call, but the So line's 'the CFO in most deals' stretches 4 of 8 (half) into most, and a belief held exactly at the bar with 8 people still reads 'Holding up'.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 8 at a bar of 6, a lean from 8 people. Half (4 of 8) said the CFO would have to agree, so plan for the CFO in about half your deals; the project executive wasn't asked about.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside 5 of 8 under 2 weeks or not needed against a bar of 6 of 8, 1 short, so I know the call and the number that made it.
screens.why_b2: The bands are counted over 8 operations leads, the marker sits at 6, and the band starting at my 2 weeks is labelled as its low edge and counted against, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: It is my Procore check, my 2 weeks and my contractor operations leads, the belief I checked going in.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a Procore check of 2 weeks to a month and where to find what would take the time, which is concrete enough to act on in the sales cycle.
screens.why_b5: The firm past-tense "Did not hold" (where the other cards said "Not holding up") and "plan for a cycle of that length" lean harder than 5 of 8 on 8 people, one person short, can carry, though the count line does say it is a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Not holding up, just: 5 of 8 say under 2 weeks or not needed, one short of 6; 3 expect 2 weeks to a month, so have the Procore proof ready to shorten that check.

screens.why_b1: The card says "Did not hold" with "3 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 3 short" right beside it, so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The four bars count my eight operations leads by answer, and the strip shows 3 for, 5 against, with the marker at 6 of 8, so what is counted, over how many, and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: It is my Commitment belief, start a paid pilot on one site, with the contractor's operations lead as the decider I named; the doubled "if it were offered today" and the clipped "You said start a paid pilot" are only rough edges.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the 5 of 8 and sends me to another tab; it does not point out that nobody took the free look on sample data, which tells me a free taster does not open the door and the pilot's price is the sticking point.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible and "a lean, not a call" is said, but "What they would start with instead" assumes the five who said no have some other first step, which two flat Nos do not show.
screens.instead: 3 of 8 would start a paid pilot on one site, and none would take a free look on sample data first, so the free step does not win anyone over; with 8 answering this is a lean, and what the five who said no would want first is on the Insights tab.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Not holding up / Did not hold) with the deciding count beside it, such as 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, or 3 of 8 said yes, 3 short.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment are my dimensions, and the belief lines ($800 to $1,000 per site a month, the Procore check within about 2 weeks, a paid pilot on one site) are the ones I checked.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what the failures mean for Fresco: no line on pricing per active super, offering a free month on one job, or leading with the hours my supers lose, even though the quotes point straight at all three.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and nothing is called strong, but the Purchase friction and Commitment boxes ask a question and show no answers, with 'never saw it' and 'asked on Price' unexplained, so Renee's free-trial quote under Price is not clearly my Commitment answer.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: per-user pricing instead of per-site, a free month on one job before paying, buyers who can't name what logs cost ('show me the hours'), a $600-a-month overtime ceiling, and liability fear about an app writing the legal record.
screens.instead: Price fails because buyers count the cost per site and can't see the hours, not because they doubt the app: try a free month on one job and pricing per active super, and lead the pitch with the 30-plus hours a month your supers already spend (5 of 7). Say plainly that the Purchase friction and Commitment whys were asked on Price.

screens.why1: As the person who would pay for this, I need the idea in front of me before any buying questions, so opening with it makes sense.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, action items, Procore or ACC are all words I use every week, and 'AI scribe' is clear enough.
screens.why3: My supers do site walks and fight to get notes and photos into Procore, so I can picture this on my jobs.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The belief line, 'it would be the scribe for your site walk', just repeats the name and doesn't say what it changes, and the daily log record of the day's work it is meant to keep never comes up; the site walk is my supers' and the notes and action items are theirs, not mine.
screens.why6: Heard once it's a lot: four 'how' sentences instead of one, 'assignees' is a mouthful, and the last line ends without telling me anything new to hold onto.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an AI scribe for site walks. Your supers talk over short videos on the walk, and it turns them into the daily log with photos, who owns each item and when it's due, texts the crew their items, and sends it all to Procore or ACC. The people building it believe it would save your supers the evening spent writing up the log.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what the daily log already costs us is the obvious first buying question for the person who pays for the software.
screens.why2: Daily log, site and hours are words I use every day, and I can take it in on one hearing.
screens.why3: I sign off on the tools but don't fill in the logs, so I'd be estimating my supers' hours per site from what they tell me rather than knowing it.
screens.why4: An open hours box with None as zero and I can't recall as the one escape covers every honest answer without overlap.
screens.why5: It asks the founder's hours per site a month on the daily log in plain words, and nothing of the product or the founder's labels for people comes through.
screens.why6: One short question, a number to give, and one escape said last; easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: The box is in the founder's own unit, base and period (hours per site, last month). Any answer of 30 or more counts for and anything under 30, None included, counts against, and I can't recall is the one escape.

screens.why1: I'm the one who pays for job-site tools, so right after the idea card and how much time my sites lose to the daily log, asking what it's worth to me is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: A monthly price per site is how we already buy software for our jobs, so I can answer this on first read.
screens.why3: I set and sign off on per-site software spend against our project budgets, so I can put a number on this from my own books.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap and run from cheap to well past anything I'd pay, with a clear 'wouldn't pay' option and 'I can't say' kept apart.
screens.why5: All that reaches me is the idea card shown on purpose and the name Fresco, with nothing of the founder's plan or terms for people slipping into the question or the options.
screens.why6: Spoken it is one short question, then four options I can hold, then the escape, and the follow-up is just two bands on the side I picked.
screens.why7: Every option is a monthly price per site, there are five bands plus 'I wouldn't pay for this' with a band edge exactly at the founder's $800 low, two bands and 'wouldn't pay' count against and three count for, and 'I can't say' is the only escape, set apart.

screens.why1: Right after I put a number on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: It reads my answer back as I'd say it, about $500 to $800 a site a month, and the question is plain.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need to see from my supers and my Procore setup before I'd pay more per site, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Fresco was named on the idea card, and nothing new about the founder's product or terms is slipped in here.
screens.why6: One short question with a read-back that says cleanly aloud; the dollar range comes out naturally.

screens.why1: Right after I named my price, asking whether I can approve it myself or need the CFO is the obvious next question for the person who buys the software.
screens.why2: Sign off and the CFO are everyday words at a GC, so I'd answer it on the first read.
screens.why3: I know my approval limit and when a software spend goes up to the CFO, so I'm answering from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The four go cleanly from me alone, to the CFO, to several people, to not my call; I can't say fits as the escape, and none of them overlap.
screens.why5: It asks about a price and the CFO in words any GC uses, with nothing of the product's pitch or odd terms reaching me.
screens.why6: Short, one either-or question with four short options read as a list and one escape, so it is easy to hold by ear.
screens.why7: One measure (who has to agree), the fixed four in order from alone to someone else's call with the CFO named second, no Yes or No in front, and I can't say as the only escape, so the belief can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $800 per site a month across all your jobs yourself, or would the CFO have to agree? -- same four options and I can't say, because per site times twenty jobs is the number the CFO actually looks at.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether the CFO has to sign off, asking what else stands between me and buying is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Procore is the system every one of our jobs runs on, so a check that a new tool works with it is plain to me, even if I'd call it testing the Procore integration.
screens.why3: I've put apps from the Procore marketplace through our IT and project admins before, so I know roughly how long that check takes us.
screens.why4: The bands cover everything and 'It wouldn't be needed' plus 'I can't tell' fit, but a check of exactly a month could be either '2 weeks to 1 month' or '1 to 3 months'.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch or terms leaks through; it names the product and a step in my own world, Procore.
screens.why6: Short question, four options I can hold, the escape said last, then a simple two-way follow-up, and nothing only the eye can read.
screens.why7: Every option is on the one measure, how long the step takes; the edge sits at 2 weeks with '1 to under 2 weeks' below it; two bands plus 'not needed' count for and three bands count against, so the belief can go either way; the only escape is 'I can't tell'.
